summary: Cleveland Motley describes building a playground swing set that generates electricity: swingers turn a drive shaft via roller clutches, which drives a bicycle-hub-based axial flux generator adapted from Hugh Piggott's design. The project was a collaboration with Ryan Alpers. After a gear change to 112 teeth, the setup produced around 9 volts consistently at the Bay Area Makers Faire, powering 12 volt LEDs, 9 volt EL wire and a 9 volt keyboard, though the author hoped for 12 volts with an additional gear reduction.
one_line: An Instructable detailing how to convert a donated playground swing set into a generator that produces electricity from swingers' motion.
key_facts: Cleveland Motley built a swing set that generates electricity, published as a Workshop project in the Energy category.
The design adapted Hugh Piggott's axial flux permanent magnet generator, which the author had previously built and adapted to a stationary bicycle.
Roller clutches let the swingers turn the drive shaft only on their forward swing, while the roller clutches freewheel on the return trip.
The swing set was donated by a friend's parents and was made of 1/4 inch steel.
The magnet rotor plates weigh at least 45 pounds and act as a flywheel, smoothing the power output.
The generator's stator was mounted independently of the rotors so chain tension could be adjusted with dynamic drop outs.
At the Bay area Makers Faire on 5/21/11, replacing the 44 tooth driven gear with a 112 tooth gear allowed the swing set to produce around 9 volts consistently.
At 6 volts the swing set produced 0.3 Amps and 1.2 Watts.
The swing set ran 12 volt LEDs, 9 volt EL wire and a 9 volt electric keyboard at the same time at the Makers Faire.
Before the gear change, the author produced around 4.5 to 6 volts DC with two large adults swinging hard.
The generator's AC output is converted to DC by bridge rectifiers housed in a box of wires hanging out of the stator.
The author found that pretty short swinger chains gave the best power output.
The author stated the project needed an additional gear reduction to consistently produce 12 volts.
Materials included 4 pillow blocks, 4 roller clutches, 9ft of keyed drive shaft, around 20ft of angle iron, and motorcycle chain.
The author thanked Reid Johnston, Matt Gil, Baker, and the people at Bearing Agencies in SF for technical insight, and Cork Marcheschi for use of his studio and equipment.
